Averaging Rotations

Sulley
2024-01-11
数学 - 图形学
四元数, 插值, 数学, 旋转, 特征向量, 线性代数, 计算机, 随笔

Averaging rotations (i.e., quaternions) may not be as simple as you expected. Based on the result of this work, this post goes into the details why a simple weighted average of quaternions does not work and how to implement the real interpolation between quaternions. Part of this post is inspired from Quaternion Weighted Average. Thank Daniel.

Method #1: Simple Weighted Average of Quaternions

Problem Definition

Before I go into the details of today’s topic, let me first give a relatively formal definition to the problem I will discuss in the later sections.

(Weighted Average of Rotations) Given a set of rotations (quaternions) q1,q2,⋯ ,qnq_1, q_2, \cdots, q_nq1​,q2​,⋯,qn​ and their associated weights α1,α2,⋯ ,αn\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \cdots, \alpha_nα1​,α2​,⋯,αn​ where ∑iαi=1\sum_i\alpha_i=1∑i​αi​=1 and αi≥0\alpha_i\ge 0αi​≥0, we would like to calculate the weighted average rotation q~=f(q1,⋯ ,qn,α1,⋯ ,αn)\tilde{q}=f(q_1, \cdots, q_n, \alpha_1, \cdots, \alpha_n)q~​=f(q1​,⋯,qn​,α1​,⋯,αn​) such that
(1) q~\tilde{q}q~​ is continuous at each qiq_iqi​ with fixed (α1,⋯ ,αn)(\alpha_1, \cdots, \alpha_n)(α1​,⋯,αn​);
(2) q~\tilde{q}q~​ is continuous at each αi\alpha_iαi​ with fixed (q1,⋯ ,qn)(q_1,\cdots,q_n)(q1​,⋯,qn​).

This definition points out for a desired weighted average of rotations, we would like it to maintain robust to slight changes of any of the sub-rotations and to slight changes of weights. As we will see soon, however, most popular solutions do not adhere to these two properties, and thus creating the so-called jump rotation phenomenon.

N-lerp: Normalized Arithmetic Average

N-lerp is short for Normalized Interpolation. It’s a widely-used, simple quaterion interpolation strategy to blend multiple quaternions. Basically, an N-lerped quaternion q~nl\tilde{q}_\text{nl}q~​nl​ can be calculated as:

q~nl=∑i=1nαiqi∥∑i=1nαiqi∥\tilde{q}_\text{nl} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_iq_i}{\Vert \sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_iq_i\Vert} q~​nl​=∥∑i=1n​αi​qi​∥∑i=1n​αi​qi​​

The norm at the denominator is necessary to make sure q~nl\tilde{q}_\text{nl}q~​nl​ is a unit quaternion, thus representing a rotation.

To see what’s wrong with the simple N-lerp method, let’s look at simple case.

Assume we are interpolating two quaternions, one is a fixed identity quaternion, i.e., qid=(1,0,0,0)q_\text{id}=(1, 0, 0, 0)qid​=(1,0,0,0). The second is a quaternion qqq simply rotating around the z\mathbf{z}z axis, i.e., the world up direction. But in the following examples, the rotation axis of qqq will slightly deviate from the world up direction z=(0,0,1)\mathbf{z}=(0, 0, 1)z=(0,0,1) so as to let you see how the rotation axis and angle will change as rotation changes. We also set α1=α2=1/2\alpha_1=\alpha_2=1/2α1​=α2​=1/2.

As a result, the final interpolated quaternion will be:

q~nl=12qid+12q∥12qid+12q∥\tilde{q}_\text{nl} = \frac{\frac{1}{2}q_\text{id}+\frac{1}{2}q}{\Vert\frac{1}{2}q_\text{id}+\frac{1}{2}q\Vert} q~​nl​=∥21​qid​+21​q∥21​qid​+21​q​

The pesudo code is given as follows:

The right panel shows the rotation of the second quaternion, which represents a camera always looking at the cube from the player’s view. I also print qqq’s rotation axis and angle, along with its www component (real part of the quaternion).

We can see that, when the rotation angle is in [0,π)[0, \pi)[0,π), the rotation axis is just the world up direction (as I said, with slight deviation) z=(0,0,1)\mathbf{z}=(0,0,1)z=(0,0,1), which can be justified by the z value printed on screen. However, when the rotation angle surpasses π\piπ, the rotation axis suddenly flips over to the inverse world up direction, as shown by the negative z value. This means that, when the rotation angle is between [π,2π)[\pi, 2\pi)[π,2π), the rotation axis will be flipped and the interpolated quaternion will lie in the other half space of the plane.

The following figure shows what is means to say the other half space of the plane.

When rotation angle is in [0,π)[0, \pi)[0,π), q~nl\tilde{q}_\text{nl}q~​nl​ sweeps through the top right quarter of the plane, and when rotation angle is in [π,2π)[\pi, 2\pi)[π,2π), q~nl\tilde{q}_\text{nl}q~​nl​ sweeps through the top left quarter of the plane. Merging both, only the top half space of the plane will be covered by q~nl\tilde{q}_\text{nl}q~​nl​. The bottom half space, will never have the chance to reach. This is where the jump rotation comes from: the jump change of the rotation axis changes the direction the quaternion is interpolated, and thus changes the final interpolated quaternion.

You may ask, why does the rotation axis have to be flipped? Can you just maintain the rotation axis and let the rotation angle span [0,2π)[0, 2\pi)[0,2π)? Good question! But it will still cause jump rotation at where angle 000 or 2π2\pi2π, in which case the interpolated quaternion will only span the right half space of the plane. The same problem again.

In fact, we can take a closer look at the the we compute q~nl\tilde{q}_\text{nl}q~​nl​. Let’s try to derive a closed form of it.

Assume qid=(1,0,0,0)q_\text{id}=(1, 0, 0, 0)qid​=(1,0,0,0) and q=(cos⁡(θ/2),sin⁡(θ/2)n)q=(\cos(\theta/2), \sin(\theta/2)\mathbf{n})q=(cos(θ/2),sin(θ/2)n), where θ∈[0,2π)\theta\in [0, 2\pi)θ∈[0,2π) is the rotation angle of quaternion qqq. In the simple case above, n=z=(0,0,1)\mathbf{n}=\mathbf{z}=(0, 0, 1)n=z=(0,0,1), but in fact it can be any unit rotation axis.

Then we have the following derivations:

q~nl=12qid+12q∥12qid+12q∥=qid+q∥qid+q∥=(1+cos⁡(θ/2),sin⁡((θ/2))n)∥(1+cos⁡(θ/2),sin⁡((θ/2))n)∥=12cos⁡(θ/4)(1+cos⁡(θ/2),sin⁡((θ/2))n)=(1+cos⁡(θ/2)2cos⁡(θ/4),sin⁡((θ/2)2cos⁡(θ/4)n)=(cos⁡(θ/4),sin⁡(θ/4)n)\begin{aligned} \tilde{q}_\text{nl} &= \frac{\frac{1}{2}q_\text{id}+\frac{1}{2}q}{\Vert\frac{1}{2}q_\text{id}+\frac{1}{2}q\Vert}\\ &= \frac{q_\text{id}+q}{\Vert q_\text{id}+q\Vert}\\ &= \frac{(1+\cos(\theta/2), \sin((\theta/2))\mathbf{n})}{\Vert(1+\cos(\theta/2), \sin((\theta/2))\mathbf{n}) \Vert}\\ &= \frac{1}{2\cos(\theta/4)}(1+\cos(\theta/2), \sin((\theta/2))\mathbf{n})\\ &= \left(\frac{1+\cos(\theta/2)}{2\cos(\theta/4)}, \frac{\sin((\theta/2)}{2\cos(\theta/4)}\mathbf{n}\right)\\ &= (\cos(\theta/4), \sin(\theta/4)\mathbf{n}) \end{aligned} q~​nl​​=∥21​qid​+21​q∥21​qid​+21​q​=∥qid​+q∥qid​+q​=∥(1+cos(θ/2),sin((θ/2))n)∥(1+cos(θ/2),sin((θ/2))n)​=2cos(θ/4)1​(1+cos(θ/2),sin((θ/2))n)=(2cos(θ/4)1+cos(θ/2)​,2cos(θ/4)sin((θ/2)​n)=(cos(θ/4),sin(θ/4)n)​

The final quaternion q~nl\tilde{q}_\text{nl}q~​nl​ spans over half of the rotation range of qqq, meaning that it either spans over [0,π)[0, \pi)[0,π) if θ∈[0,2π)\theta\in [0, 2\pi)θ∈[0,2π), or spans [−π/2,π/2)[-\pi/2, \pi/2)[−π/2,π/2) if θ∈[−π,π)\theta\in [-\pi, \pi)θ∈[−π,π). This is exactly what we can expect from what we’ve discussed above.

This can be easily extended to multiple quaternions. More quaternions there are, more prone to slight changes the average quaternion will be.

S-lerp: Spherical Average

If you are familiar with spherical interpolation (S-lerp), you may wonder if it’s possible to maintain continuity using S-lerp. Unfortunately, the jump rotation issue will still arise even if you use S-lerp.

Let’s use the same example of N-lerp. The first quaternion is qid=(1,0,0,0)q_\text{id}=(1, 0, 0, 0)qid​=(1,0,0,0), and assume the second quaternion as q=(cos⁡(θ/2),sin⁡(θ/2)n)q=(\cos(\theta/2), \sin(\theta/2)\mathbf{n})q=(cos(θ/2),sin(θ/2)n). The weights are 1/21/21/2 for both qidq_\text{id}qid​ and qqq. By the definition of S-lerp (I use the vanilla S-lerp definition for simplicity), we have the S-lerped quaternion q~sl\tilde{q}_\text{sl}q~​sl​:

q~sl=(qqid∗)12qid=q12=(cos⁡(θ/4),sin⁡(θ/4)n)=q~nl\begin{aligned} \tilde{q}_\text{sl} &= (qq_\text{id}^*)^\frac{1}{2}q_\text{id}\\ &= q^\frac{1}{2}\\ &= (\cos(\theta/4), \sin(\theta/4)\mathbf{n})\\ &= \tilde{q}_\text{nl} \end{aligned} q~​sl​​=(qqid∗​)21​qid​=q21​=(cos(θ/4),sin(θ/4)n)=q~​nl​​

This result is equivalent to N-lerp, which is not surprising as S-lerp is still manipulating raw quaternions.

We can use the following figure to illustrate why N-lerp and S-lerp are not working in our trivial case:

The angle of the result quaternion q~nl\tilde{q}_\text{nl}q~​nl​ is a periodic function with respect to the rotation angle of qqq. Though we stipulate that angle θ\thetaθ is within [0,2π)[0, 2\pi)[0,2π), we can actually extend it to R\mathbb{R}R by adding a period of 2π2\pi2π. But in the game engine, the value will be reduced into [0,2π)[0, 2\pi)[0,2π). It’s clear that at the point of x=2kπx=2k\pix=2kπ, the function is discontinuous, i.e., f(2kπ)−=πf(2k\pi)_-=\pif(2kπ)−​=π while f(2kπ)+=0f(2k\pi)_+=0f(2kπ)+​=0, and this therefore causes the jump rotation issue.

Discontinuity of N-lerp

In this section, I will go deeper into the mathematical details of the jump rotation problem, formally proving that simple weighted average with either N-lerp or S-lerp will sometimes (and when) cause the jump rotation problem. This can help us determine in which situations you can safely use N-lerp or S-lerp to average quaternions.

Theorem 1: Quaternion Discontinuity of N-lerp

First, we present a lemma, and it will be used to introduce our theorem.

Lemma 1.1: Given two quaternions q1,q2q_1, q_2q1​,q2​ and their weights 0<α1,α2<10<\alpha_1,\alpha_2< 10<α1​,α2​<1, their N-lerp average quaternion q~=α1q1+α2q2∥α1q1+α2q2∥\tilde{q}=\dfrac{\alpha_1q_1+\alpha_2q_2}{\Vert\alpha_1q_1+\alpha_2q_2\Vert}q~​=∥α1​q1​+α2​q2​∥α1​q1​+α2​q2​​, which is a function of q1q_1q1​, is discontinuous at rotation angle 0 (2π)0~(2\pi)0 (2π) when θ2≠0 (2π)\theta_2\not=0~(2\pi)θ2​=0 (2π), assuming the range angle is [0,2π][0, 2\pi][0,2π] where 2π2\pi2π also represents zero rotation.

To prove this lemma, we first rewrite the quaternions as q1=[cos⁡(θ1/2),sin⁡(θ1/2)n1],q2=[cos⁡(θ2/2),sin⁡(θ2/2)n2]q_1=[\cos(\theta_1/2),\sin(\theta_1/2)\mathbf{n}_1], q_2=[\cos(\theta_2/2),\sin(\theta_2/2)\mathbf{n}_2]q1​=[cos(θ1​/2),sin(θ1​/2)n1​],q2​=[cos(θ2​/2),sin(θ2​/2)n2​]. Then, their weighted average is:

α1q1+α2q2=[α1cos⁡(θ1/2)+α2cos⁡(θ2/2),α1sin⁡(θ1/2)n1+α2sin⁡(θ2/2)n2]\alpha_1q_1+\alpha_2q_2=[\alpha_1\cos(\theta_1/2)+\alpha_2\cos(\theta_2/2), \alpha_1\sin(\theta_1/2)\mathbf{n}_1+\alpha_2\sin(\theta_2/2)\mathbf{n}_2] α1​q1​+α2​q2​=[α1​cos(θ1​/2)+α2​cos(θ2​/2),α1​sin(θ1​/2)n1​+α2​sin(θ2​/2)n2​]

and its norm is:

∥α1q1+α2q2∥=α12+α22+2α1α2(cos⁡(θ12)cos⁡(θ22)+sin⁡(θ12)sin⁡(θ22)n1⋅n2)\Vert\alpha_1q_1+\alpha_2q_2\Vert= \sqrt{ \alpha_1^2+\alpha_2^2+2\alpha_1\alpha_2\left(\cos\left(\frac{\theta_1}{2}\right)\cos\left(\frac{\theta_2}{2}\right)+\sin\left(\frac{\theta_1}{2}\right)\sin\left(\frac{\theta_2}{2}\right)\mathbf{n}_1\cdot\mathbf{n}_2\right) } ∥α1​q1​+α2​q2​∥=α12​+α22​+2α1​α2​(cos(2θ1​​)cos(2θ2​​)+sin(2θ1​​)sin(2θ2​​)n1​⋅n2​)​

which gives the explicit expression of q~\tilde{q}q~​:

q~=[α1cos⁡(θ1/2)+α2cos⁡(θ2/2)∥α1q1+α2q2∥,α1sin⁡(θ1/2)n1+α2sin⁡(θ2/2)n2∥α1q1+α2q2∥]\tilde{q}=\left[\frac{\alpha_1\cos(\theta_1/2)+\alpha_2\cos(\theta_2/2)}{\Vert\alpha_1q_1+\alpha_2q_2\Vert}, \frac{\alpha_1\sin(\theta_1/2)\mathbf{n}_1+\alpha_2\sin(\theta_2/2)\mathbf{n}_2}{\Vert\alpha_1q_1+\alpha_2q_2\Vert} \right]q~​=[∥α1​q1​+α2​q2​∥α1​cos(θ1​/2)+α2​cos(θ2​/2)​,∥α1​q1​+α2​q2​∥α1​sin(θ1​/2)n1​+α2​sin(θ2​/2)n2​​]

If q~\tilde{q}q~​ is continuous at θ1=2π\theta_1=2\piθ1​=2π, or θ1=0\theta_1=0θ1​=0, then it must satisfy that:

q~(θ1=0)=q~(θ1=2π)\tilde{q}(\theta_1=0)=\tilde{q}(\theta_1=2\pi) q~​(θ1​=0)=q~​(θ1​=2π)

with any given α1,α2\alpha_1, \alpha_2α1​,α2​ and θ2\theta_2θ2​.

We only need to compare to the real part of q~\tilde{q}q~​:

Re (q~(θ1=0))=Re (q~(θ1=2π))α1+α2cos⁡(θ2/2)∥α1q1+α2q2∥=−α1+α2cos⁡(θ2/2)∥α1q1+α2q2∥α1+α2cos⁡(θ2/2)α12+α22+2α1α2cos⁡(θ2/2)=−α1+α2cos⁡(θ2/2)α12+α22−2α1α2cos⁡(θ2/2)\begin{aligned} \text{Re}~(\tilde{q}(\theta_1=0))&=\text{Re}~(\tilde{q}(\theta_1=2\pi))\\ \frac{\alpha_1+\alpha_2\cos(\theta_2/2)}{\Vert\alpha_1q_1+\alpha_2q_2\Vert}&=\frac{-\alpha_1+\alpha_2\cos(\theta_2/2)}{\Vert\alpha_1q_1+\alpha_2q_2\Vert}\\ \frac{\alpha_1+\alpha_2\cos(\theta_2/2)}{\sqrt{\alpha_1^2+\alpha_2^2+2\alpha_1\alpha_2\cos(\theta_2/2)}}&=\frac{-\alpha_1+\alpha_2\cos(\theta_2/2)}{\sqrt{\alpha_1^2+\alpha_2^2-2\alpha_1\alpha_2\cos(\theta_2/2)}} \end{aligned} Re (q~​(θ1​=0))∥α1​q1​+α2​q2​∥α1​+α2​cos(θ2​/2)​α12​+α22​+2α1​α2​cos(θ2​/2)​α1​+α2​cos(θ2​/2)​​=Re (q~​(θ1​=2π))=∥α1​q1​+α2​q2​∥−α1​+α2​cos(θ2​/2)​=α12​+α22​−2α1​α2​cos(θ2​/2)​−α1​+α2​cos(θ2​/2)​​

Taking square on both sides and simplifying the equation, we have:

cos⁡(θ22)(1−cos⁡2(θ22))=0\cos\left(\frac{\theta_2}{2}\right)\left(1-\cos^2\left(\frac{\theta_2}{2}\right)\right)=0 cos(2θ2​​)(1−cos2(2θ2​​))=0

implying that the equality holds only when θ2=0\theta_2=0θ2​=0 or θ2=π\theta_2=\piθ2​=π or θ2=2π\theta_2=2\piθ2​=2π. The solution of θ2=π\theta_2=\piθ2​=π is discarded by substituting θ2=π\theta_2=\piθ2​=π into the equation above. When θ2=0\theta_2=0θ2​=0 or 2π2\pi2π, both sides represent the identity quaternion.

In other words, if θ2≠0 (2π)\theta_2\not=0~(2\pi)θ2​=0 (2π), this equation does not hold, and thus, q~\tilde{q}q~​ is not continuos at θ1=0 (2π)\theta_1=0~(2\pi)θ1​=0 (2π).

We can actually estimate the difference of angle between q~(θ1=0)\tilde{q}(\theta_1=0)q~​(θ1​=0) and q~(θ1=2π)\tilde{q}(\theta_1=2\pi)q~​(θ1​=2π). This gives us an intuitive impression of to which extent the rotation will jump. For ease of computation, we take the difference of the squared real parts:

    Re2(q~(θ1=0))−Re2(q~(θ1=2π))=cos⁡2(ϕθ1=0)−cos⁡2(ϕθ1=2π)=(α1+α2cos⁡(θ2/2))2α12+α22+2α1α2cos⁡(θ2/2)−(−α1+α2cos⁡(θ2/2))2α12+α22−2α1α2cos⁡(θ2/2)=4α1α23cos⁡(θ2/2)sin⁡2(θ2/2)(α12+α22+2α1α2cos⁡(θ2/2))(α12+α22−2α1α2cos⁡(θ2/2))\begin{aligned} &~~~~\text{Re}^2(\tilde{q}(\theta_1=0)) - \text{Re}^2(\tilde{q}(\theta_1=2\pi))\\ &= \cos^2(\phi_{\theta_1=0})-\cos^2(\phi_{\theta_1=2\pi})\\ &= \frac{(\alpha_1+\alpha_2\cos(\theta_2/2))^2}{\alpha_1^2+\alpha_2^2+2\alpha_1\alpha_2\cos(\theta_2/2)}-\frac{(-\alpha_1+\alpha_2\cos(\theta_2/2))^2}{\alpha_1^2+\alpha_2^2-2\alpha_1\alpha_2\cos(\theta_2/2)}\\ &= \frac{4\alpha_1\alpha_2^3\cos(\theta_2/2)\sin^2(\theta_2/2)}{(\alpha_1^2+\alpha_2^2+2\alpha_1\alpha_2\cos(\theta_2/2))(\alpha_1^2+\alpha_2^2-2\alpha_1\alpha_2\cos(\theta_2/2))} \end{aligned} ​    Re2(q~​(θ1​=0))−Re2(q~​(θ1​=2π))=cos2(ϕθ1​=0​)−cos2(ϕθ1​=2π​)=α12​+α22​+2α1​α2​cos(θ2​/2)(α1​+α2​cos(θ2​/2))2​−α12​+α22​−2α1​α2​cos(θ2​/2)(−α1​+α2​cos(θ2​/2))2​=(α12​+α22​+2α1​α2​cos(θ2​/2))(α12​+α22​−2α1​α2​cos(θ2​/2))4α1​α23​cos(θ2​/2)sin2(θ2​/2)​​

where ϕθ1=0\phi_{\theta_1=0}ϕθ1​=0​ and ϕθ1=2π\phi_{\theta_1=2\pi}ϕθ1​=2π​ are respectively the half rotation angle of quaternion formed by substituting θ1=0\theta_1=0θ1​=0 and θ1=2π\theta_1=2\piθ1​=2π. Assuming α2=α1\alpha_2=\alpha_1α2​=α1​, the above equation simplifies to:

Re2(q~(θ1=0))−Re2(q~(θ1=2π))=cos⁡(θ22)\text{Re}^2(\tilde{q}(\theta_1=0)) - \text{Re}^2(\tilde{q}(\theta_1=2\pi))=\cos\left(\frac{\theta_2}{2}\right) Re2(q~​(θ1​=0))−Re2(q~​(θ1​=2π))=cos(2θ2​​)

This means that the magnitude of rotation jump is related to the cosine of θ2\theta_2θ2​.

Theorem 1: Given quaternions q1,⋯ ,qnq_1, \cdots, q_nq1​,⋯,qn​ and their α1,⋯ ,αn\alpha_1, \cdots, \alpha_nα1​,⋯,αn​ where 0<α1,⋯ ,αn<10<\alpha_1, \cdots, \alpha_n<10<α1​,⋯,αn​<1 and α1+⋯+αn=1\alpha_1+\cdots+\alpha_n=1α1​+⋯+αn​=1, the N-lerp average quaternion q~=α1q1+⋯+αnqn∥α1q1+⋯+αnqn∥\tilde{q}=\dfrac{\alpha_1q_1+\cdots+\alpha_nq_n}{\Vert\alpha_1q_1+\cdots+\alpha_nq_n\Vert}q~​=∥α1​q1​+⋯+αn​qn​∥α1​q1​+⋯+αn​qn​​, which is a function of q1q_1q1​, has discontinuous at angle 0 (2π)0~(2\pi)0 (2π) when the rotation angle of quaternion α2q2+⋯+αnqn∥α2q2+⋯+αnqn∥\dfrac{\alpha_2q_2+\cdots+\alpha_nq_n}{\Vert\alpha_2q_2+\cdots+\alpha_nq_n\Vert}∥α2​q2​+⋯+αn​qn​∥α2​q2​+⋯+αn​qn​​ is not 0 (2π)0~(2\pi)0 (2π), assuming the range angle is [0,2π][0, 2\pi][0,2π] where 2π2\pi2π also represents zero rotation.

This can be seen by decomposing q~\tilde{q}q~​ to:

Applying Lemma 1.1, Theorem 1 is obvious.

Theorem 1 tells us that the N-lerp style average quaternion q~\tilde{q}q~​ will be discontinuous at least at 000, where quaternion suddenly changes its rotation angle from 2π2\pi2π. For most cases, you cannot make sure the quaternion formed by other sub-quaternions has a rotation angle of zero, so you need to do something to relax Theorem 1 so that there will be less chance for q~\tilde{q}q~​ to jump rotate.

The following figure shows that even if sub-quaternions are fixed, changing their weights could also drastically change the final average quaternion, resulting in the jump rotation issue.

Method #2: Matrix Decomposition for the Largest Eigen-value

The jump rotation problem is rooted in the double cover property of quaternions, i.e., qqq and −q-q−q represent the same rotation, so that quaternions provide a 2:1 mapping of the rotation group. Ideally, changing the sign of qqq should not change the result average, but as we’ve observed above, it indeed changes the result, which is not what we would want.

We would like a way, serving as a 1:1 mapping to the rotation group, to help us disambiguate from the double cover issue. Matrix, does serve this purpose!

Special Orthogonal Matrix Is 1:1 Mapping to Rotation

First according to Wikipedia, we call the subgroup of orthogonal matrices with determinant +1 the special orthogonal group, denoted by SO(3)\textrm{SO}(3)SO(3). Then we can easily see that every rotation can be represented uniquely by a matrix M∈SO(3)M\in\textrm{SO}(3)M∈SO(3). This can be proved by showing that any rotation is a linear transformation of the standard basis x,y,z\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}, \mathbf{z}x,y,z, which can be represented by a matrix in SO(3)\textrm{SO}(3)SO(3). For the inverse, any matrix M∈SO(3)M\in\textrm{SO}(3)M∈SO(3) forms a unique orthonormal basis representing a unique rotation upon the standard basis.

Next, we prove that the group of quaternions is 2:1 mapping to SO(3)\textrm{SO}(3)SO(3). This is obvious because the matrix presentation of a quaternion q=(x,y,z,w)q=(x, y, z, w)q=(x,y,z,w) is:

Q=[1−2y2−2z22xy−2zw2xz+2yw2xy+2zw1−2x2−2z22yz−2xw2xz−2yw2yz+2xw1−2x2−2y2]∈SO(3)Q=\begin{bmatrix} 1-2y^2-2z^2 & 2xy-2zw & 2xz+2yw\\ 2xy+2zw & 1-2x^2-2z^2 & 2yz-2xw\\ 2xz-2yw & 2yz+2xw & 1-2x^2-2y^2 \end{bmatrix} \in\textrm{SO}(3) Q=⎣⎢⎡​1−2y2−2z22xy+2zw2xz−2yw​2xy−2zw1−2x2−2z22yz+2xw​2xz+2yw2yz−2xw1−2x2−2y2​⎦⎥⎤​∈SO(3)

This is a rotation around vector (x,y,z)(x,y,z)(x,y,z) by a angle of 2θ2\theta2θ with cos⁡(θ)=w\cos(\theta)=wcos(θ)=w. It’s clear that both qqq and −q-q−q are mapped to QQQ.

We can comprehend quaternions as the process of rotation, whereas conceive matrices as the result of rotation, represented as the basis after rotation.

Problem Reformulation

Till now, the problem becomes: given a set of rotation matrices and their associated weights, how do we compute the average rotation? We can first give a particular definition of average: the average rotation should minimize a weighted sum of the squared Frobenius norms of the rotation matrices. This definition can be formulated as follows:

q~=arg⁡min⁡q∑i=1nαi∥Q(q)−Q(qi)∥F2\tilde{q}=\arg\min_{q}\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i\Vert Q(q)-Q(q_i)\Vert^2_F q~​=argqmin​i=1∑n​αi​∥Q(q)−Q(qi​)∥F2​

Based on this definition, we can derive a very neat closed form of q~\tilde{q}q~​, which maintains a nice property of continuity of interest. I call this method, M-lerp, short for Matrix Interpolation for rotations, and call the final quaternion as q~ml\tilde{q}_\text{ml}q~​ml​.

In the next subsection, I will go into the details of deriving q~ml\tilde{q}_\text{ml}q~​ml​ step by step, basically following this work, but with more elaborations on some of the missing steps.

Solving the Problem

Let’s first expand q~ml\tilde{q}_\text{ml}q~​ml​ in the form of matrices:

This implies that the average quaternion that minimizes the weighted sum of Frobenius norms actually minimizes the weighted sum of squared sines of half angles, which is quite intuitive to interpret q~ml\tilde{q}_\text{ml}q~​ml​.

There are plenty of algorithms to compute the largest eigenvalue of a symmetric matrix, but the most commonly used one is power iteration, as it’s simple to implement and fast in most cases.

I won’t go into the details of power iteration. You can easily understand this algorithm with basic linear algebra knowledge.

However, M-lerp does not provide continuity on [0,2π][0,2\pi][0,2π] either. Before going into analysis why and when M-lerp is not working, I give a very simple example to illustrate why M-lerp does not necessarily provide continuity.

Why Is M-lerp Working

NOTE: When reviewing this section, I find the proofs of Theorem 3 and Theorem 4 are NOT correct. Therefore, M-lerp does NOT ensure continuity for either each rotation or each weight. The incorrect proofs are still left below for reference.

Using the same notion of continuity, we conclude that the matrix decomposition method quite well maintains the property of continuity. This can be formalized as the following theorems.

Theorem 3: Quaternion Continuity of M-lerp

Without loss of generality, we view q~ml\tilde{q}_\text{ml}q~​ml​ as a function of q1q_1q1​, i.e., q~(q1)=arg⁡max⁡qq⊤Mq\tilde{q}(q_1)=\arg\max_{q} q^\top Mqq~​(q1​)=argmaxq​q⊤Mq where M=∑i=1nαiqiqi⊤M=\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_iq_iq_i^\topM=∑i=1n​αi​qi​qi⊤​. We will show that this function is continuous on q1q_1q1​.

For ease of illustration, we rewrite MMM as M=αqq⊤+∑i=1nαiqiqi⊤M=\alpha qq^\top+\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i q_iq_i^\topM=αqq⊤+∑i=1n​αi​qi​qi⊤​ where all variables are fixed except qqq. Then, the average quaternion will be q~=arg⁡max⁡q′q′⊤Mq′\tilde{q}=\arg\max_{q'}q'^\top Mq'q~​=argmaxq′​q′⊤Mq′.

We first show that the mapping from a real symmetric matrix MMM to its largest eigenvalue λ\lambdaλ is continuous.

Lemma 3.1: The mapping from a real symmetric matrix MMM to its largest eigenvalue λmax(M)\lambda_\text{max}(M)λmax​(M) is continuous.

We begin with that fact that the spectral norm of MMM is given by its largest singular value, which is the square root of the largest eigenvalue of MM⊤MM^\topMM⊤. Since MMM is symmetric, we have MM⊤=M2MM^\top=M^2MM⊤=M2, and its largest eigenvalue is the squared largest eigenvalue of MMM, and thus the spectral norm of MMM is MMM’s largest eigenvalue.

On the other hand, we know that the spectral norm map is continuous, and thus the map M↦∥M∥2=λmax(M)M\mapsto \Vert M\Vert_2=\lambda_\text{max}(M)M↦∥M∥2​=λmax​(M) is continuous.

Then, we prove the following lemma.

Lemma 3.2: The mapping from a unit vector qqq to matrix M=qq⊤M=qq^\topM=qq⊤ is continuous regarding the Frobenius norm.

Assume q0q_0q0​ is any unit vector and M0=q0q0⊤M_0=q_0q_0^\topM0​=q0​q0⊤​. For ∀ϵ>0\forall \epsilon >0∀ϵ>0 and qqq close enough to q0q_0q0​ (in terms of the angle between qqq and q0q_0q0​):

Corollary 3.1: The mapping from a unit vector qqq to matrix M=αqq⊤+∑i=1nαiqiqi⊤M=\alpha qq^\top+\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i q_iq_i^\topM=αqq⊤+∑i=1n​αi​qi​qi⊤​ is continuous regarding the Frobenius norm, where α,α1,⋯ ,αn\alpha, \alpha_1, \cdots, \alpha_nα,α1​,⋯,αn​ are fixed coefficients and q1,⋯ ,qnq_1, \cdots, q_nq1​,⋯,qn​ are fixed unit vectors.

Lemma 3.3: The mapping from a unit vector qqq to the eigenvector of the largest eigenvalue of M=qq⊤M=qq^\topM=qq⊤ is continuous. That is, q↦umaxq\mapsto u_\text{max}q↦umax​ is continuous, where Mumax=λmaxumaxMu_\text{max}=\lambda_\text{max}u_\text{max}Mumax​=λmax​umax​.

In fact, the matrix M=qq⊤M=qq^\topM=qq⊤ has only one non-zero eigenvalue, 1, and its eigenvector is qqq. Proof is quite simple:

Mu=λu⇒qq⊤u=λu⇒(q⊤u)q=λu Mu=\lambda u\Rightarrow qq^\top u=\lambda u\Rightarrow (q^\top u)q=\lambda u Mu=λu⇒qq⊤u=λu⇒(q⊤u)q=λu

λαq=(αq⊤q)q⇒λαq=αq⇒λ=1\lambda\alpha q=(\alpha q^\top q)q\Rightarrow \lambda\alpha q=\alpha q\Rightarrow \lambda=1 λαq=(αq⊤q)q⇒λαq=αq⇒λ=1

and any vector parallel to qqq is the eigenvector. For simplicity, we take u=qu=qu=q as the eigenvector. This ends our proof.

Remarks: It seems that this is a special case of a more general theorem. Please refer to Kato, T., Perturbation theory for linear operators. Springer-Verlag, 1976. I am not 100% sure about the correctness of the proof. This continuity may stem from the floating number error induced in the course of numerical calculation.

We can say that the averaged rotation is C0C^0C0 continuous but not C1C^1C1 continuous. I do not know if this statement is true. It’s only my conjecture.

λ−λ0→0\lambda-\lambda_0\to0 λ−λ0​→0

where λ\lambdaλ is the largest eigenvalue of M′M'M′ and λ0\lambda_0λ0​ is the largest eigenvalue of M0′=M0+MfixedM_0'=M_0+M_\text{fixed}M0′​=M0​+Mfixed​ where M0=α0qq⊤M_0=\alpha_0 qq^\topM0​=α0​qq⊤. It follows that:

u⊤(M+Mfixed)u−u0⊤(M0+Mfixed)u0→0u^\top (M+M_\text{fixed})u-u_0^\top(M_0+M_\text{fixed})u_0\to 0 u⊤(M+Mfixed​)u−u0⊤​(M0​+Mfixed​)u0​→0

Method #3: Quaternion Flipping

The most common implementation of averaing rotations might be to maintain a running average qrq_\text{r}qr​ and flip any incoming sub-rotation qqq if the dot product between qrq_\text{r}qr​ and qqq is negative, i.e., it’s on the opposite hemisphere to the running average.

In this section, I will show that this method also introduces discontinuity in most cases, but it indeed grants continuity under certain conditions. If these conditions are satisfied in your application, you can safely use this approach to average rotations. We call this method F-lerp.

Theorem 5: Conditional Continuity of F-lerp

We first present a special case of F-lerp to give you an intuitive insight of how F-lerp ensures continuity.

Theorem 5: Given nnn quaternions qi=[cos⁡(θi/2),sin⁡(θi/2)ni] (i=1,⋯ ,n)q_i=[\cos(\theta_i/2), \sin(\theta_i/2)\mathbf{n}_i]~(i=1,\cdots,n)qi​=[cos(θi​/2),sin(θi​/2)ni​] (i=1,⋯,n) and their weights αi (i=1,⋯ ,n)\alpha_i~(i=1,\cdots,n)αi​ (i=1,⋯,n) with αi≥0\alpha_i\ge 0αi​≥0, their F-lerp average rotation q~fl\tilde{q}_\text{fl}q~​fl​ is continuous about qℓq_\ellqℓ​ at θℓ=0 (2π)\theta_\ell=0~(2\pi)θℓ​=0 (2π) for some ℓ∈{1,2,⋯ ,n}\ell\in\{1,2,\cdots,n\}ℓ∈{1,2,⋯,n}. All weights and other quaternions are fixed.

Proof is quite simple. assume the unnormalized quaternion in the ℓ−1\ell-1ℓ−1-th iteration of F-lerp is q~ℓ−1=∑i=1ℓ−1αisiqi=[∑i=1ℓ−1αisicos⁡(θi/2),∑i=1ℓ−1αisisin⁡(θi/2)ni]\tilde{q}_{\ell-1}=\sum_{i=1}^{\ell-1}\alpha_is_iq_i=[\sum_{i=1}^{\ell-1}\alpha_is_i\cos(\theta_i/2),\sum_{i=1}^{\ell-1}\alpha_i s_i\sin(\theta_i/2)\mathbf{n}_i]q~​ℓ−1​=∑i=1ℓ−1​αi​si​qi​=[∑i=1ℓ−1​αi​si​cos(θi​/2),∑i=1ℓ−1​αi​si​sin(θi​/2)ni​], where sis_isi​ can be +1+1+1 or −1-1−1 according to the F-lerp algorithm.
When θℓ=0\theta_\ell=0θℓ​=0, the ℓ\ellℓ-th quaternion will be qℓ=[1,0,0,0]q_\ell=[1,0,0,0]qℓ​=[1,0,0,0], so the product between qℓq_\ellqℓ​ and q~ℓ−1\tilde{q}_{\ell-1}q~​ℓ−1​ is ∑i=1ℓ−1αisicos⁡(θi/2)\sum_{i=1}^{\ell-1}\alpha_is_i\cos(\theta_i/2)∑i=1ℓ−1​αi​si​cos(θi​/2). We can assume it’s non-negative, so in the ℓ\ellℓ-th iteration of F-lerp the unnormalized quaternion is q~ℓ=q~ℓ−1+αℓqℓ=[∑i=1ℓ−1αisicos⁡(θi/2)+αℓ,∑i=1ℓ−1αisisin⁡(θi/2)ni]\tilde{q}_\ell=\tilde{q}_{\ell-1}+\alpha_\ell q_\ell=[\sum_{i=1}^{\ell-1}\alpha_is_i\cos(\theta_i/2)+\alpha_\ell,\sum_{i=1}^{\ell-1}\alpha_is_i\sin(\theta_i/2)\mathbf{n}_i]q~​ℓ​=q~​ℓ−1​+αℓ​qℓ​=[∑i=1ℓ−1​αi​si​cos(θi​/2)+αℓ​,∑i=1ℓ−1​αi​si​sin(θi​/2)ni​]. Then for θℓ=2π\theta_\ell=2\piθℓ​=2π, qℓ=[−1,0,0,0]q_\ell=[-1,0,0,0]qℓ​=[−1,0,0,0], so the product will be negative, so the sign of qℓq_\ellqℓ​ will be flipped to −1-1−1. The unnormalized quaternion in the ℓ\ellℓ-th iteration of F-lerp will now become q~ℓ=q~ℓ−1−αℓqℓ=[∑i=1ℓ−1αisicos⁡(θi/2)+αℓ,∑i=1ℓ−1αisisin⁡(θi/2)ni]\tilde{q}_{\ell}=\tilde{q}_{\ell-1}-\alpha_\ell q_\ell=[\sum_{i=1}^{\ell-1}\alpha_is_i\cos(\theta_i/2)+\alpha_\ell,\sum_{i=1}^{\ell-1}\alpha_is_i\sin(\theta_i/2)\mathbf{n}_i]q~​ℓ​=q~​ℓ−1​−αℓ​qℓ​=[∑i=1ℓ−1​αi​si​cos(θi​/2)+αℓ​,∑i=1ℓ−1​αi​si​sin(θi​/2)ni​]. This is the same as when θℓ=0\theta_\ell=0θℓ​=0. Proof completes.

Theorem 5 tells us that if all quaternions except the variable one are fixed, the average rotation derived from F-lerp is continuous about this rotation at θ=0 (2π)\theta=0~(2\pi)θ=0 (2π), which is, as proved in Theorem 1, not continuous for N-lerp.

The following figure shows three rotations that are close enough are averaged without any discontinuity.

Theorem 5 rigorously assumes only one quaternion is variable. The following Corollary 5.1 presents a more general case where all quaternions are variable and the average quaternion is continuous about all of them, if satisfying certain conditions:

Corollary 5.1: Given nnn quaternions qi=[cos⁡(θi/2),sin⁡(θi/2)ni] (i=1,⋯ ,n)q_i=[\cos(\theta_i/2), \sin(\theta_i/2)\mathbf{n}_i]~(i=1,\cdots,n)qi​=[cos(θi​/2),sin(θi​/2)ni​] (i=1,⋯,n) and their weights αi (i=1,⋯ ,n)\alpha_i~(i=1,\cdots,n)αi​ (i=1,⋯,n) with αi≥0\alpha_i\ge 0αi​≥0. All weights are fixed. Assume for some ℓ∈{1,⋯ ,n}\ell\in\{1,\cdots,n\}ℓ∈{1,⋯,n} the quaternion qℓq_\ellqℓ​ lies in the neighborhood of 0 (2π)0~(2\pi)0 (2π) and all other quaternions are not near 0 (2π)0~(2\pi)0 (2π). If (1) ∀i,j≠ℓ,qi⋅qj≥0\forall i,j\not=\ell,q_i\cdot q_j\ge 0∀i,j=ℓ,qi​⋅qj​≥0, and (2) ∀i,cos⁡(θi/2)≥0\forall i,\cos(\theta_i/2)\ge 0∀i,cos(θi​/2)≥0 or cos⁡(θi/2)≤0\cos(\theta_i/2)\le 0cos(θi​/2)≤0, then the F-lerp average rotation q~fl\tilde{q}_\text{fl}q~​fl​ is continuous at (θ1,⋯ ,θn)(\theta_1,\cdots,\theta_n)(θ1​,⋯,θn​) where θℓ=0 (2π)\theta_{\ell}=0~(2\pi)θℓ​=0 (2π) and all others are not.

Corollary 5.1 tells us that if one quaternion is crossing degree 0 (2π)0~(2\pi)0 (2π) and the other quaternions are close enough (defined by two conditions: (1) their dot products are positive, and (2) their cosines have the same sign), the F-lerp result will not cause jump rotation when the quaternion crosses the boundary.

Let’s proof it.

Let Δ(θi,δ)\Delta(\theta_i,\delta)Δ(θi​,δ) be the neighborhood of the rotation angle of qiq_iqi​ with range 2δ2\delta2δ and θi∈Δ(θi,δ)\theta_i\in\Delta(\theta_i,\delta)θi​∈Δ(θi​,δ). Particularlly, Δ(θℓ,δ)=(2π−δ,2π)∪(0,δ)\Delta(\theta_\ell,\delta)=(2\pi-\delta,2\pi)\cup(0,\delta)Δ(θℓ​,δ)=(2π−δ,2π)∪(0,δ), and for i≠ℓ,Δ(θi,δ)=(θi−δ,θi+δ)⊂[0,2π]i\not=\ell, \Delta(\theta_i,\delta)=(\theta_i-\delta,\theta_i+\delta)\subset[0,2\pi]i=ℓ,Δ(θi​,δ)=(θi​−δ,θi​+δ)⊂[0,2π]. Suppose ∀i,cos⁡(θi)≥0\forall i, \cos(\theta_i)\ge0∀i,cos(θi​)≥0. We also assume also rotation axes are fixed.

The jjj-th iteration result of F-lerp can be written as (without normalization):

q~j=∑i=1jαisiqi=[∑i=1jαisicos⁡(θi/2),∑i=1jαisisin⁡(θi/2)ni]\tilde{q}_j=\sum_{i=1}^j\alpha_is_iq_i=\left[\sum_{i=1}^j\alpha_is_i\cos(\theta_i/2),\sum_{i=1}^j\alpha_is_i\sin(\theta_i/2)\mathbf{n}_i\right] q~​j​=i=1∑j​αi​si​qi​=[i=1∑j​αi​si​cos(θi​/2),i=1∑j​αi​si​sin(θi​/2)ni​]

When j=ℓ−1j=\ell-1j=ℓ−1, it’s easy to know that q~j=∑i=1ℓ−lαiqi\tilde{q}_{j}=\sum_{i=1}^{\ell-l}\alpha_iq_iq~​j​=∑i=1ℓ−l​αi​qi​ according to the first condition.

When j=ℓj=\ellj=ℓ, we examine the value of q~ℓ\tilde{q}_\ellq~​ℓ​ respectively for θℓ=0\theta_\ell=0θℓ​=0 and θℓ=2π\theta_\ell=2\piθℓ​=2π. It can be proved that q~ℓ\tilde{q}_\ellq~​ℓ​ is the same one, since we have q~ℓ(θℓ=0)=q~ℓ−1+[αℓ,0,0,0]\tilde{q}_\ell(\theta_\ell=0)=\tilde{q}_{\ell-1}+[\alpha_\ell,0,0,0]q~​ℓ​(θℓ​=0)=q~​ℓ−1​+[αℓ​,0,0,0] and q~ℓ(θℓ=2π)=q~ℓ−1−[−αℓ,0,0,0]=q~ℓ(θℓ=0)\tilde{q}_\ell(\theta_\ell=2\pi)=\tilde{q}_{\ell-1}-[-\alpha_\ell,0,0,0]=\tilde{q}_\ell(\theta_\ell=0)q~​ℓ​(θℓ​=2π)=q~​ℓ−1​−[−αℓ​,0,0,0]=q~​ℓ​(θℓ​=0).

When j>ℓj>\ellj>ℓ, we can prove that q~j=∑i=1ℓ−1αiqi+[αℓ,0,0,0]+∑i=ℓ+1jαiqi\tilde{q}_j=\sum_{i=1}^{\ell-1}\alpha_iq_i+[\alpha_\ell,0,0,0]+\sum_{i=\ell+1}^j\alpha_iq_iq~​j​=∑i=1ℓ−1​αi​qi​+[αℓ​,0,0,0]+∑i=ℓ+1j​αi​qi​. Taking j=nj=nj=n, we can find that q~n\tilde{q}_nq~​n​ is continuous at (θ1,⋯ ,0,⋯ ,θn)⊤(\theta_1,\cdots,0,\cdots,\theta_n)^\top(θ1​,⋯,0,⋯,θn​)⊤ that satistify the two conditions in the neighborhood.

You can similarly prove that if ∀i,cos⁡(θi)≤0\forall i, \cos(\theta_i)\le0∀i,cos(θi​)≤0, q~n=∑i=1ℓ−1αiqi−[αℓ,0,0,0]+∑i=ℓ+1nαiqi\tilde{q}_n=\sum_{i=1}^{\ell-1}\alpha_iq_i-[\alpha_\ell,0,0,0]+\sum_{i=\ell+1}^n\alpha_iq_iq~​n​=∑i=1ℓ−1​αi​qi​−[αℓ​,0,0,0]+∑i=ℓ+1n​αi​qi​ at (θ1,⋯ ,0,⋯ ,θn)⊤(\theta_1,\cdots,0,\cdots,\theta_n)^\top(θ1​,⋯,0,⋯,θn​)⊤.

We have the following Corollary 5.2 to slightly relax the first condition of Corollary 5.1:

Corollary 5.2: Given nnn quaternions qi=[cos⁡(θi/2),sin⁡(θi/2)ni] (i=1,⋯ ,n)q_i=[\cos(\theta_i/2), \sin(\theta_i/2)\mathbf{n}_i]~(i=1,\cdots,n)qi​=[cos(θi​/2),sin(θi​/2)ni​] (i=1,⋯,n) and their weights αi (i=1,⋯ ,n)\alpha_i~(i=1,\cdots,n)αi​ (i=1,⋯,n) with αi≥0\alpha_i\ge 0αi​≥0. All weights are fixed. Assume for some ℓ∈{1,⋯ ,n}\ell\in\{1,\cdots,n\}ℓ∈{1,⋯,n} the quaternion qℓq_\ellqℓ​ lies in the neighborhood of 0 (2π)0~(2\pi)0 (2π) and all other quaternions are not near 0 (2π)0~(2\pi)0 (2π). The F-lerp average rotation q~fl\tilde{q}_\text{fl}q~​fl​ is continuous at (θ1,⋯ ,θn)(\theta_1,\cdots,\theta_n)(θ1​,⋯,θn​) where θℓ=0 (2π)\theta_{\ell}=0~(2\pi)θℓ​=0 (2π) and all others are not, if the following conditions are satisfied:
(1) {q1,⋯ ,qℓ−1,qℓ+1,⋯ ,qn}\{q_1,\cdots,q_{\ell-1},q_{\ell+1},\cdots,q_n\}{q1​,⋯,qℓ−1​,qℓ+1​,⋯,qn​} can be partitioned into two sets A={qμ1,⋯ ,qμτ}A=\{q_{\mu_1},\cdots,q_{\mu_\tau}\}A={qμ1​​,⋯,qμτ​​} and B={qω1,⋯ ,qωϕ}B=\{q_{\omega_1},\cdots,q_{\omega_\phi}\}B={qω1​​,⋯,qωϕ​​} and the two sets satisfy:
(1.1) ∀qi,qj∈A,qi⋅qj≥0\forall q_i,q_j\in A, q_i\cdot q_j\ge 0∀qi​,qj​∈A,qi​⋅qj​≥0,
(1.2) ∀qi,qj∈B,qi⋅qj≥0\forall q_i,q_j\in B, q_i\cdot q_j\ge 0∀qi​,qj​∈B,qi​⋅qj​≥0.
(1.3) ∀qi∈A∀qj∈B,qi⋅qj<0\forall q_i\in A \forall q_j\in B, q_i\cdot q_j <0∀qi​∈A∀qj​∈B,qi​⋅qj​<0.
(2) ∀qi∈A,cos⁡(θi/2)≥0\forall q_i\in A,\cos(\theta_i/2)\ge 0∀qi​∈A,cos(θi​/2)≥0 or cos⁡(θi/2)≤0\cos(\theta_i/2)\le 0cos(θi​/2)≤0, and ∀qj∈B,cos⁡(θj/2)≤0\forall q_j\in B,\cos(\theta_j/2)\le 0∀qj​∈B,cos(θj​/2)≤0 or cos⁡(θj/2)≥0\cos(\theta_j/2)\ge 0cos(θj​/2)≥0.

The second condition says that the cosines of quaternions in the same set have the same sign, but the consines of quaternions from different sets are different.

Corollary 5.2 can be proved by progressively considering q~j\tilde{q}_jq~​j​ from j<ℓj<\ellj<ℓ, j=ℓj=\ellj=ℓ and j>ℓj>\ellj>ℓ. You should focus on the current sign of each quaternion qjq_jqj​ added to q~j\tilde{q}_jq~​j​.

Corollary 5.2 tells us that if all quaternions can be divided into two sets where (1) the intra-dot product is positive ( quaternions in the same set are close enough), (2) the inter-dot product is negative (quaternions from different sets are far away from each other), and (3) their rotation angles can also be separated by their cosine values, F-lerp then ensures continuity.

If you have a set of quaternions that are very close to each other, or two sets of quaternions that are separatable, you can use F-lerp to smoothly average quaternions.

Theorem 6: Discontinuity of F-lerp

In this section, I will show you that F-lerp also introduces discontinuities while eliminating some discontinuities brought by N-lerp. We have the following Theorem 6.

Theorem 6: Given nnn quaternions qi=[cos⁡(θi/2),sin⁡(θi)ni]q_i=[\cos(\theta_i/2),\sin(\theta_i)\mathbf{n}_i]qi​=[cos(θi​/2),sin(θi​)ni​] and their associated weights αi (i=1,⋯ ,n)\alpha_i~(i=1,\cdots,n)αi​ (i=1,⋯,n) with αi≥0\alpha_i\ge 0αi​≥0, the result of F-lerp has discontinuities if satisfying (1) q~n−1⋅qn=0\tilde{q}_{n-1}\cdot q_n=0q~​n−1​⋅qn​=0, and (2) there exists a neighborhood of θn\theta_nθn​ that makes the dot product change its sign, assuming q1,⋯ ,qn−1q_1,\cdots,q_{n-1}q1​,⋯,qn−1​ and all αi\alpha_iαi​ are fixed and qnq_nqn​ is variable. Here q~n−1=[cos⁡(θ~n−1/2),sin⁡(θ~n−1/2)n~n−1]\tilde{q}_{n-1}=[\cos(\tilde{\theta}_{n-1}/2),\sin(\tilde{\theta}_{n-1}/2)\tilde{\mathbf{n}}_{n-1}]q~​n−1​=[cos(θ~n−1​/2),sin(θ~n−1​/2)n~n−1​] is the quaternion derived from the n−1n-1n−1-th iteration of the F-lerp algorithm.

The intuition behind Theorem 6 is that as qnq_nqn​ is continuous regarding all its elements, there should be some points at which the dot product between q~n−1\tilde{q}_{n-1}q~​n−1​ and qnq_nqn​ changes its sign in the neighbourhood, i.e., from positive to negative or from negative to positive. This causes a significant difference between the two consecutive quaternions, giving rise to jump rotation.
Note that by default, q~n−1\tilde{q}_{n-1}q~​n−1​ refers to the normalized result of the F-lerp algorithm though normalization is only applied at the final step in the original algorithm.

The key point is to find qnq_nqn​ that makes q~n−1⋅qn=0\tilde{q}_{n-1}\cdot q_n=0q~​n−1​⋅qn​=0. According to the definition of q~n−1\tilde{q}_{n-1}q~​n−1​ and qnq_nqn​, this gives us:

cos⁡(θ~n−12)cos⁡(θn2)+sin⁡(θ~n−12)sin⁡(θn2)n~n−1⋅nn=0\cos\left(\frac{\tilde{\theta}_{n-1}}{2}\right)\cos\left(\frac{\theta_n}{2}\right)+\sin\left(\frac{\tilde{\theta}_{n-1}}{2}\right)\sin\left(\frac{\theta_n}{2}\right)\tilde{\mathbf{n}}_{n-1}\cdot\mathbf{n}_n=0 cos(2θ~n−1​​)cos(2θn​​)+sin(2θ~n−1​​)sin(2θn​​)n~n−1​⋅nn​=0

which implies that θn=π\theta_n=\piθn​=π might be a discontinuity regardless of nn\mathbf{n}_nnn​.

and

This example satisfies the equation given at the beginning and there exists ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0 such that in (3π/2−ε,3π/2+ε)(3\pi/2-\varepsilon,3\pi/2+\varepsilon)(3π/2−ε,3π/2+ε) the dot product changes its sign.

The following figure illustrates that discontinuity does not appear at θ=0 (2π)\theta=0~(2\pi)θ=0 (2π) but at a point that makes the dot product zero. Jump rotation occurs.

The question, however, arises that any quaternion qqq that makes the dot product zero is always a discontinuity? The answer is not always, but very likely to happen. If we assume n=n~n−1\mathbf{n}=\tilde{\mathbf{n}}_{n-1}n=n~n−1​, we can simplify the equation:

    cos⁡(θ~n−12)cos⁡(θn2)+sin⁡(θ~n−12)sin⁡(θn2)n~n−1⋅nn=cos⁡(θ~n−12)cos⁡(θn2)+sin⁡(θ~n−12)sin⁡(θn2)=cos⁡(θ~n−1−θn2)\begin{aligned} &~~~~\cos\left(\frac{\tilde{\theta}_{n-1}}{2}\right)\cos\left(\frac{\theta_n}{2}\right)+\sin\left(\frac{\tilde{\theta}_{n-1}}{2}\right)\sin\left(\frac{\theta_n}{2}\right)\tilde{\mathbf{n}}_{n-1}\cdot\mathbf{n}_n\\ &=\cos\left(\frac{\tilde{\theta}_{n-1}}{2}\right)\cos\left(\frac{\theta_n}{2}\right)+\sin\left(\frac{\tilde{\theta}_{n-1}}{2}\right)\sin\left(\frac{\theta_n}{2}\right)\\ &=\cos\left(\frac{\tilde{\theta}_{n-1}-\theta_n}{2}\right) \end{aligned} ​    cos(2θ~n−1​​)cos(2θn​​)+sin(2θ~n−1​​)sin(2θn​​)n~n−1​⋅nn​=cos(2θ~n−1​​)cos(2θn​​)+sin(2θ~n−1​​)sin(2θn​​)=cos(2θ~n−1​−θn​​)​

The root of it is θn=θ~n−1±π\theta_n=\tilde{\theta}_{n-1}\pm\piθn​=θ~n−1​±π, one of the two is within [0,2π][0,2\pi][0,2π]. If n≠n~n−1\mathbf{n}\not=\tilde{\mathbf{n}}_{n-1}n=n~n−1​, it will get more complicated but there must also be discontinuities.

Remarks: F-lerp can be very helpful if you have a set of quaternions that are very close or two sets of quaternions that are separatable, but the risk is the result can be prone to discontinuities that are not 0 (2π)0~(2\pi)0 (2π), as shown in Theorem 6. If your quaternions are all around 0 (2π)0~(2\pi)0 (2π), F-lerp can be a very good choice – it’s smooth, fast, and will not trigger discontinuity.

Method #4: Smoothing the Discontinuity

C-lerp: Circular Mean as a Way of Average

Okay let’s now forget about everything and think the very first question: why jump rotation happens? The answer is the illness of angle representation. The angle representation in game engine is [0,2π][0,2\pi][0,2π] or [−π,π][-\pi,\pi][−π,π], both representing a full circle. In either case, we cannnot simply use the arithmetic mean to average angles because it’s undirectional.

What about transforming the trivial angle representation into some other representation that is continuous regarding the input angle? Trigonometric functions, particularly cosine and sine functions, as we all know, serve this purpose quite well, since cos⁡(0)=cos⁡(2π)\cos(0)=\cos(2\pi)cos(0)=cos(2π) and sin⁡(0)=sin⁡(2π)\sin(0)=\sin(2\pi)sin(0)=sin(2π).

Therefore, given a set of angles, we can first map them to the unit circle, i.e., converting from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, compute the arithmetic mean of these points, and them map the averaged point back to the angle representation. This will be the final average angle we want.

More formally, assume θ1,⋯ ,θn∈[0,2π]\theta_1,\cdots,\theta_n\in[0,2\pi]θ1​,⋯,θn​∈[0,2π] are nnn angles, we can use the following formula to calculate the average angle θˉ\bar{\theta}θˉ:

θˉ=atan2(1n∑i=1nsin⁡θi,1n∑i=1ncos⁡θi)=atan2(∑i=1nsin⁡θi,∑i=1ncos⁡θi)\bar{\theta}=\text{atan2}\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\sin\theta_i,\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\cos\theta_i\right)=\text{atan2}\left(\sum_{i=1}^n\sin\theta_i,\sum_{i=1}^n\cos\theta_i\right) θˉ=atan2(n1​i=1∑n​sinθi​,n1​i=1∑n​cosθi​)=atan2(i=1∑n​sinθi​,i=1∑n​cosθi​)

If each angle θi\theta_iθi​ is weighted by αi\alpha_iαi​, then the average angle would be:

θˉ=atan2(∑i=1nαisin⁡θi,∑i=1nαicos⁡θi)\bar{\theta}=\text{atan2}\left(\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i\sin\theta_i,\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i\cos\theta_i\right) θˉ=atan2(i=1∑n​αi​sinθi​,i=1∑n​αi​cosθi​)

This method is called C-lerp, short for circular interpolation, directly from the concept of Circular Mean.

We can write the pseudo code like:

The following figure gives two examples of how C-lerp works:

First, two angles θ1,θ2\theta_1,\theta_2θ1​,θ2​ are mapped to their Cartesian coordiantes (cos⁡θ1,sin⁡θ1)(\cos\theta_1,\sin\theta_1)(cosθ1​,sinθ1​) and (cos⁡θ2,sin⁡θ2)(\cos\theta_2,\sin\theta_2)(cosθ2​,sinθ2​). Then the xxx axis and yyy axis values are independetly averaged as (cos⁡θˉ,sin⁡θˉ)=(cos⁡θ1+cos⁡θ22,sin⁡θ1+sin⁡θ22)(\cos\bar{\theta},\sin\bar{\theta})=\left(\dfrac{\cos\theta_1+\cos\theta_2}{2},\dfrac{\sin\theta_1+\sin\theta_2}{2}\right)(cosθˉ,sinθˉ)=(2cosθ1​+cosθ2​​,2sinθ1​+sinθ2​​). Last, arctan is applied to convert the average point back to polar coordinates.

Looks perfect, right? However, unfortunately vanilla C-lerp does NOT ensure continuity. As a simple example, take θ1=0\theta_1=0θ1​=0 and θ=θ2\theta=\theta_2θ=θ2​ as a variable. According to C-lerp, the average angle would be:

θˉ=atan2(sin⁡θ,1+cos⁡θ)=arctan⁡(sin⁡θ1+cos⁡θ)=arctan⁡(tan⁡(θ2))\bar{\theta}=\text{atan2}(\sin\theta,1+\cos\theta)=\arctan\left(\dfrac{\sin\theta}{1+\cos\theta}\right)=\arctan\left(\tan\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\right) θˉ=atan2(sinθ,1+cosθ)=arctan(1+cosθsinθ​)=arctan(tan(2θ​))

It is obvious that arctan⁡(tan⁡(θ/2))\arctan(\tan(\theta/2))arctan(tan(θ/2)) is discontinuous at θ=π\theta=\piθ=π. When θ→π−,θˉ→π/2\theta\to\pi_-,\bar{\theta}\to\pi/2θ→π−​,θˉ→π/2, whereas θˉ→−π/2\bar{\theta}\to-\pi/2θˉ→−π/2 as θ→π+\theta\to\pi_+θ→π+​. All the discontinuity is rooted in the discontinuity of the atan2\text{atan2}atan2 function, though cos⁡(⋅)\cos(\cdot)cos(⋅) and sin⁡(⋅)\sin(\cdot)sin(⋅) are continuous.

The following figure shows this discontinuity.

Albeit discontinuous at some points, C-lerp can replace L-lerp and F-lerp in most cases as there is less chance to trigger such discontinuity.

SC-lerp: Smoothed C-lerp

How to mitigate this sort of discontinuity caused by zero divided by zero? The most intuitive solution is to add a small positive number ε\varepsilonε on the denominator side so that the denominator will always be positive, i.e.,

θˉ=atan2(sin⁡θ,1+cos⁡θ+ε)=arctan⁡(sin⁡θ1+cos⁡θ+ε), ε>0\bar{\theta}= \text{atan2}(\sin\theta,1+\cos\theta+\varepsilon) = \arctan\left(\frac{\sin\theta}{1+\cos\theta+\varepsilon}\right),~ \varepsilon>0 θˉ=atan2(sinθ,1+cosθ+ε)=arctan(1+cosθ+εsinθ​), ε>0

You can verify that θˉ\bar{\theta}θˉ is continuous about θ\thetaθ, as shown in the following figure.

and here is the result:

Now the rotation becomes smooth at θ=π\theta=\piθ=π because the denominator will never get to zero and continuity is granted. But you may ask what about θ1\theta_1θ1​ is not equal to 0 but π\piπ instead. In this case, θˉ\bar{\theta}θˉ is calculated as follows:

θˉ=atan2(sin⁡θ,cos⁡θ−1+ε), ε>0\bar{\theta}=\text{atan2}(\sin\theta,\cos\theta-1+\varepsilon),~ \varepsilon>0 θˉ=atan2(sinθ,cosθ−1+ε), ε>0

Note that we cannot simply expand atan2\text{atan2}atan2 as arctan⁡\arctanarctan since the denominator can become negative. Without loss of generality, let’s assume θ∈[−π,0]\theta\in[-\pi,0]θ∈[−π,0] and the root for equation cos⁡θ−1+ε=0\cos\theta-1+\varepsilon=0cosθ−1+ε=0 is θ′=−arccos⁡(1−ε)\theta'=-\arccos(1-\varepsilon)θ′=−arccos(1−ε). Therefore, when θ∈[θ′,0]\theta\in[\theta',0]θ∈[θ′,0], the denominator is positive, and the result can be expressed as:

θˉ=arctan⁡(sin⁡θcos⁡θ−1+ε), ε>0\bar{\theta}=\arctan\left(\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta-1+\varepsilon}\right),~ \varepsilon>0 θˉ=arctan(cosθ−1+εsinθ​), ε>0

but when θ∈[−π,θ′]\theta\in[-\pi, \theta']θ∈[−π,θ′], both the nominator and the denominator are negative, so the equation becomes:

θˉ=arctan⁡(sin⁡θcos⁡θ−1+ε)−π, ε>0\bar{\theta}=\arctan\left(\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta-1+\varepsilon}\right)-\pi,~ \varepsilon>0 θˉ=arctan(cosθ−1+εsinθ​)−π, ε>0

Taking limits for both equations:

lim⁡θ→θ+′θˉ=−π2lim⁡θ→θ−′θˉ=−π2\begin{aligned} \lim_{\theta\to\theta'_+}\bar{\theta}&=-\frac{\pi}{2}\\ \lim_{\theta\to\theta'_-}\bar{\theta}&=-\frac{\pi}{2} \end{aligned} θ→θ+′​lim​θˉθ→θ−′​lim​θˉ​=−2π​=−2π​​

meaning that θˉ\bar{\theta}θˉ is continous on [−π,0][-\pi,0][−π,0]. You can similarly prove that it is also continous on [0,π][0,\pi][0,π], and hence is continuous on [−π,π][-\pi,\pi][−π,π].

The following figure shows its continuity on [−π,0][-\pi,0][−π,0]:

You can tweak the parameter ε\varepsilonε to control how smooth the rotation will be at the root point. The larger ε\varepsilonε is, the more smooth the result will be, but comes at the cost of curvature and accuracy.

In this secion, I present Theorem 7 to show when SC-lerp is continuous and discontinuous.

Theorem 7: Given nnn angles θ1,⋯ ,θn\theta_1,\cdots,\theta_nθ1​,⋯,θn​ where θi∈[−π,π]\theta_i\in[-\pi,\pi]θi​∈[−π,π] and the associated non-negative weights αi≥0\alpha_i\ge 0αi​≥0, the SC-lerped average angle is defined as θˉε=atan2(∑i=1nαisin⁡θi,∑i=1nαicos⁡θi+ε)\bar{\theta}_\varepsilon=\text{atan2}(\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i\sin\theta_i,\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i\cos\theta_i+\varepsilon)θˉε​=atan2(∑i=1n​αi​sinθi​,∑i=1n​αi​cosθi​+ε), where ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0. Let y(θ1)=∑i=1nαisin⁡θiy(\theta_1)=\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i\sin\theta_iy(θ1​)=∑i=1n​αi​sinθi​ and x(θ1)=∑i=1nαicos⁡θi+εx(\theta_1)=\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i\cos\theta_i+\varepsilonx(θ1​)=∑i=1n​αi​cosθi​+ε. Then:
θˉε\bar{\theta}_\varepsilonθˉε​ is continuous about each angle on domain [−π,π][-\pi,\pi][−π,π] if any of the following conditions is met:

(2) ∑i=1nαicos⁡θi+ε<0\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i\cos\theta_i+\varepsilon<0∑i=1n​αi​cosθi​+ε<0 holds on [−π,π][-\pi,\pi][−π,π].

where sss is defined similar to the sign function:

Case 4.3
θ∗∉{0,±π/2,±π}\theta^*\not\in\{0,\pm\pi/2,\pm\pi\}θ∗∈{0,±π/2,±π}. In this case, both x(θ1)x(\theta_1)x(θ1​) and y(θ1)y(\theta_1)y(θ1​) change the signs. lim⁡θ1→θ∗sin⁡θ1−sin⁡θ∗cos⁡θ1−cos⁡θ∗=−lim⁡θ1→01tan⁡(θ1/2+θ∗)=−1tan⁡(θ∗)\lim_{\theta_1\to\theta^*}\frac{\sin\theta_1-\sin\theta^*}{\cos\theta_1-\cos\theta^*}=-\lim_{\theta_1\to0}\frac{1}{\tan(\theta_1/2+\theta^*)}=-\frac{1}{\tan(\theta^*)} θ1​→θ∗lim​cosθ1​−cosθ∗sinθ1​−sinθ∗​=−θ1​→0lim​tan(θ1​/2+θ∗)1​=−tan(θ∗)1​

To be short, θˉε\bar{\theta}_\varepsilonθˉε​ is discontinuous at θ∗∈[−π,π]\theta^*\in[-\pi,\pi]θ∗∈[−π,π] such that x(θ∗)=0x(\theta^*)=0x(θ∗)=0 and y(θ∗)=0y(\theta^*)=0y(θ∗)=0 and θ∗∈{0,±π}\theta^*\in\{0,\pm\pi\}θ∗∈{0,±π}. In other cases, θˉε\bar{\theta}_\varepsilonθˉε​ is continuous.

A decent value of ε\varepsilonε depends on the circumstances you are in. ε\varepsilonε can be positive or negative, and it can be large or small. Generally, if you set a relatively large ε\varepsilonε, e.g., greater than 0.80.80.8 or smaller than −0.8-0.8−0.8, that θˉε\bar{\theta}_\varepsilonθˉε​ is discontinuous will be much less likely to happen, but a large value sacrifices average precision. You should be very careful of ε\varepsilonε and tweak it for different situations.

The next three figures illustrate the results when ε\varepsilonε is respectively 000, 0.20.20.2 and 0.40.40.4. You will have a better understanding of how ε\varepsilonε makes a difference to the final rotation.

Conclusion

In this article, I discussed several methods to average rotations: N-lerp (S-lerp), M-lerp, F-lerp, C-lerp and SC-lerp. I investigated the pros and cons of each method and proposed C-lerp and its improved version SC-lerp to average rotations in a simpler and more efficient way.

In summary, I suggest you:

  • Use N-lerp if all sub-rotations are close enough and none of them cross from 000 to 2π2\pi2π (or from π\piπ to −π-\pi−π);
  • Use F-lerp if all sub-rotations are close enough or can be divided into two sets that are separatable;
  • Use M-lerp if you want a smooth and accurate result;
  • Use SC-lerp if you want a smooth and accurate result that is efficient to compute and the Euler angle interpolation does not make a big difference.

There might be mistakes in this article. Feel free to contact me if you find any / want to discuss with me / have further questions.
